key_concept: The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by the crystal field splitting ($\Delta$) they produce: $I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < H_2O < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO$.
steps: Recall the spectrochemical series in increasing field strength: $I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < en \approx NH_3 < CN^- < CO$.
Place $CO$ first. It is the strongest-field ligand because it is a $\sigma$-donor and also a strong $\pi$-acceptor (back-bonding into its $\pi^*$ orbitals), which gives a very large $\Delta$.
Place $NH_3$ above $H_2O$. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so $NH_3$ is a better $\sigma$-donor and produces a larger $\Delta$.
Place $Cl^-$ last. It is a weak-field halide and a $\pi$-donor, which reduces $\Delta$.
The decreasing order is therefore $CO > NH_3 > H_2O > Cl^-$, which matches option (1).
why_not_others: Option (2) wrongly puts $H_2O$ above $NH_3$. Options (3) and (4) reverse the series by placing the weak-field ligand $Cl^-$ first and the strongest ligand $CO$ last.
common_trap: Students often place $H_2O$ above $NH_3$, or assume the negatively charged $Cl^-$ must be a stronger ligand, forgetting that $\pi$-acceptor ability matters and charge does not decide field strength.
time_saving_tip: Since $CO$ is always the strongest ligand, options (3) and (4) drop out at once. Then just check that $NH_3 > H_2O$ to pick option (1).
